<reason>Side B won decisively by dismantling Side A's economic logic and exposing fatal operational flaws in the proposition. Side A committed an early unforced error by claiming that local attendees patronize local hotels while tourists "extract" value. Side B ruthlessly exposed this inverted economics, demonstrating that under finite stadium capacity, replacing out-of-town visitors with residents starves the municipality of net-new hotel occupancy taxes and external capital. Side B brilliantly connected this to Side A's own fairness framework: because millions of residents endure the public costs of an event while only a tiny fraction can fit in the stadium, trading away tourist tax revenue for a private ticket discount forces the non-attending local majority to subsidize a deeper municipal deficit. Furthermore, Side B trapped Side A in an operational fork between resale arbitrage and turnstile gridlock, while Side A never answered the basic supply-and-demand math showing that shrinking the general-sale pool forces dynamic algorithms to surge prices even higher for remaining fans.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In [B2.3]-[B2.4], [B4.2], and [B5.1]-[B5.3], Side B demolished Side A's core economic and "sequencing" arguments by noting that tourists do not pack a city's wealth into their suitcases when they leave, that finite stadium capacity means local reservations directly displace tax-paying visitors, and that giving below-market tickets to a small subset of locals puts zero dollars into municipal budgets to cover police and infrastructure costs. Side B also landed a sharp tactical counter in [B4.1], showing that Side A's first pressure question accidentally articulated a fatal two-way dilemma against Side A's own policy.</best_rebuttal>
